title: The Gift Card Lands in December. The Debt It Creates Doesn't Clear Until It's Redeemed.
linkedin:
A gift card sale is the easiest sale your business will make this December.

No stock to pick. No delivery to arrange. The customer pays, the till rings it up, and the money lands in the account looking exactly like every other sale that month.

Here's what the bank balance doesn't tell you. A gift card isn't a completed sale. It's a liability, a promise to hand over goods or a service later, and under the accounting standards it stays off the profit and loss statement until the card is actually redeemed.

The pattern we typically see across owner-led retail, hospitality, salon and gym businesses is that the December cash gets spent as though it was already earned profit, Christmas stock, bonuses, debt repayment, while a meaningful share of it is still owed to a customer who hasn't walked back in the door yet.

The redemption timing makes it worse. Cards sold at full price in December often get redeemed during the January clearance period, against stock or services carrying a thinner margin than when the card was sold. The cash collected doesn't change. What it actually needs to cover does.

This isn't a bookkeeping problem. Your bookkeeper is almost certainly recording this correctly already. It's a visibility problem, knowing what portion of the balance is genuinely free to spend versus already spoken for.

Tracking the outstanding gift card liability as its own running total, built from actual sales and a realistic redemption rate, is a simple fix that changes how December's cash actually gets used.

With Christmas gift card and voucher sales ramping up across retail, hospitality, salons and gyms this month, it's worth a quick reminder for East Coast business owners. That money landing in your account in December isn't fully earned yet. Under standard accounting treatment, gift card proceeds are recorded as a liability, not revenue, until the card is actually redeemed.

The pattern we see often enough to flag is businesses spending the full December gift card total as though it was already profit, then finding the redemptions arrive through January and February, sometimes against stock or services carrying a thinner margin than when the card was originally sold. The cash collected stays the same. What it needs to cover shifts.

None of this means changing how you sell gift cards. It's simply worth tracking the outstanding liability as its own number, separate from your general bank balance, so you know what's genuinely free to spend heading into the new year and what's already owed against a future delivery.

If your business runs a gift card or voucher program this Christmas, read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog for a closer look at managing that cash properly.
